top.line: Pay after you see the value, not before
top.para: Most purchases are bets on future value, and often lost: gym members paid over $17 a visit when $10 was available. This newsroom tries the opposite: £5 of credit, a few pence per article, prices you set, balances that may go negative. It works where serving costs nearly nothing. The experiment is live.

in-short.line: Paying after value works where serving costs nearly nothing
in-short.para: Paying first is a bet often lost. Starting with credit and paying when you can see what you read reconnects payment to value. A static site on a CDN suits it; Wikipedia's yearly ask shows the opposite. Prices by country and visible spending would help. Seven hypotheses face review on 6 December 2026.

future.line: We buy future value and often overpay for it
future.para: Subscriptions and deals bet that each use will become cheap enough. DellaVigna and Malmendier found gym members on contracts over $70 a month attended 4.3 times, paying more than $17 a visit against a $10 pass. Cancelling is hard: the FTC's click-to-cancel rule was vacated in July 2025, and UK rules arrive in 2027.

psychology.line: Prepaying decouples payment from use; paying after recouples them
psychology.para: Prelec and Loewenstein described the pain of paying and why prepaid consumption feels free. Gourville and Soman reported a 21.5 percent no-show rate for season ticket holders against under one percent for single tickets. Paying after the value couples payment and use again, when the value makes the price feel fair.

meter.line: Readers start at £5 and may stay below zero
meter.para: Everyone starts with £5.00. New articles read to the end cost 10p, older ones 5p, by distance read. Ratings set the price from free to double, and charges can be refused. Balances can go negative without blocking. A £5 top-up link has been live since 11 October. The payment request arrives after the value.

wikipedia.line: Wikipedia asks yearly, with no value in view
wikipedia.para: Wikipedia raised US$184.5 million in 2024 to 2025 from 7.7 million donors, about US$10 each. But the lump-sum ask comes when its thousands of small benefits are invisible and never added up. Shown a year of reading, a penny an article for four hundred articles is £4, and easier to give.

where.line: It needs near-zero serving costs and visible value
where.para: Negative balances only work where an extra reader costs almost nothing, as on a static CDN site with no back end. The value must also add up visibly: a reading history across devices, valuable in itself, with billing a side effect. Even non-payers help, since their reading and ratings show what is worth writing.

fair.line: Fair local prices, visible spending and chosen extras help
fair.para: Prices should follow local purchasing power, like The Economist's Big Mac index. Showing where money goes changes behaviour: at an amusement park, pay-what-you-want photos fetched about 92 cents, but $5.33 when half went to charity. Verified facts, follow-ups and checked briefings are extras some readers, especially commercial ones, will choose.

experiment.line: Five written hypotheses face review on 6 December
experiment.para: The meter is live and real money can move. Hypotheses written in advance: a first payment within 14 days, at least 10 payers, at least three repeat payers, no disputes, and below-zero balances not driving readers away. Two more concern portable personas. The review is on 6 December 2026, reported even if nobody paid.

limits.line: No results yet; studies explain psychology, not outcomes
limits.para: There are no results; the meter has no analytics and the review is in December. Negative balances are never collected. The cited studies concern gyms, theatre and photos, not reading. Regional prices, spending views and the year-in-reading view are not built. Wikipedia's figures are its own.

sources.line: Sources: behavioural economics studies and Wikimedia's fundraising report
sources.para: From my voice memo of 14 October 2026, with quotes checked. Sources: DellaVigna and Malmendier, Paying Not to Go to the Gym (2006); Prelec and Loewenstein, The Red and the Black (1998); Gourville and Soman via the Wilson Quarterly; Gneezy via Berkeley Haas; Wikimedia's 2024-25 report; the Big Mac Index; Latham and Watkins on the FTC rule.
